views.name: pizza_orders_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id AS order_id,
  customer_id AS customer_id,
  pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  exclusions AS exclusions,
  extras AS extras,
  order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT
  order_id AS order_id,
  customer_id AS customer_id,
  pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  exclusions AS exclusions,
  extras AS extras,
  order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_customer_orders
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders c WHERE c.order_id = pizza_customer_orders.order_id)

params.when_to_use: Calculate metrics or selections at the individual order row level (one row per order_id) across all known sources of orders: use when you need the canonical, de-duplicated list of orders with their customer, pizza, exclusions, extras, and order_time. | Join order-level attributes to other tables (e.g., join to customers, runners, recipes) when you need order identifiers and basic order attributes without additional denormalization (order_id, customer_id, pizza_id, exclusions, extras, order_time). | Filter orders by time ranges, customer_id, pizza_id, or apply further per-order logic (e.g., compute order age, classify orders) because the view preserves original order_time and identifiers at the order grain. | Use as the input to reshaping or expansion steps (for example, feeding into pizza_get_extras_expanded or pizza_get_exclusions_expanded) because it provides the base fields those expansions expect.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need aggregated metrics (counts, sums, averages) grouped by anything other than order_id without explicitly aggregating after this view — using it directly in a query that assumes an already-aggregated grain will silently over- or under-count because this view returns one row per order_id (no aggregation performed). | Do not use when you need deduplicated or prioritized order rows by some other business rule beyond simple de-duplication by order_id (for example, if you need the latest/first row per order based on order_time or a source priority beyond the UNION ALL + NOT EXISTS approach). This view only merges two sources by order_id presence; it does not implement tie-breaking other than preferring pizza_clean_customer_orders rows over pizza_customer_orders when order_id exists in both. | Do not use when you need a cohort defined by runner, pizza recipe composition, or any enrichment present in sibling JOIN views — this view contains only IDs and raw exclusion/extra payloads and will miss runner or recipe attributes, causing incorrect cohort membership if those attributes are assumed present. | Do not use when you need exploded rows per extra or per exclusion (one row per extra/exclusion). The view stores extras and exclusions as supplied (likely as arrays/strings), so treating them as separate rows will be silently wrong unless you explicitly expand them (use pizza_get_extras_expanded / pizza_get_exclusions_expanded instead). | Do not use when you require the authoritative single source-of-truth beyond the simple dedupe logic implemented here; because the UNION ALL plus NOT EXISTS pattern can hide differences in other source columns, reusing this view for complex source reconciliation may miss source-specific differences.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_with_names instead when you need customer or pizza display names alongside order rows — it is a JOIN that enriches customer/pizza identifiers with readable attributes, whereas pizza_orders_base only provides IDs. | use pizza_runner_events_clean instead when you need runner event timing or runner-centric cohorts — pizza_runner_events_clean is normalized around runner events and timing, while pizza_orders_base is order-grain and lacks runner data. | use pizza_order_runner_join instead when you need the relationship between orders and runners (e.g., who delivered which order) — that sibling JOIN contains runner linkage, whereas pizza_orders_base does not. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded when you require one row per extra (exploded extras) — pizza_get_extras_expanded reshapes the extras field into per-extra rows; pizza_orders_base leaves extras as a single field and will cause mis-counting if treated as per-extra rows. | use pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you require one row per exclusion — it reshapes exclusions into individual rows; pizza_orders_base preserves exclusions as a single field and is unsafe for per-exclusion aggregation without expansion. | use pizza_recipes_base or pizza_topping_reference when you need recipe or topping-level attributes (ingredient names, standardization) — pizza_orders_base only references pizza_id and does not provide recipe/topping details necessary for composition-level analyses. | use pizza_order_rank_by_time when you need ordering or ranking of orders by time (e.g., latest order per customer or temporal rank) — pizza_order_rank_by_time provides rank semantics, while pizza_orders_base is raw rows without rank information.

views.description: Normalized view of customer orders using the cleaned orders table when available. Use this as the canonical orders table for downstream joins and aggregations (one row per order_id). Prefer pizza_clean_customer_orders but fall back to pizza_customer_orders if needed. Casts order_time through identity to keep type; exposes extras/exclusions text for downstream parsing or joins to pizza_get_extras / pizza_get_exclusions. | Use for: orders over time; counts of orders per pizza type or customer; join orders to runners, recipes, toppings, or pizza names

views.name: pizza_orders_with_names
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.order_id AS order_id,
  p.customer_id AS customer_id,
  p.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  n.pizza_name AS pizza_name,
  p.exclusions AS exclusions,
  p.extras AS extras,
  p.order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_orders_base p
LEFT JOIN pizza_names n ON n.pizza_id = p.pizza_id

params.when_to_use: Report/order-level details about each pizza line on an order — one row per order_id × pizza_id combination. | Join-ready source when you need the pizza display name (pizza_name) together with the raw order fields (customer_id, exclusions, extras, order_time) from pizza_orders_base. | Driving table for analyses that require exact order_time for each pizza item (time-series of items ordered) without changing granularity.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need one row per order (order-level aggregates) — this view is at the order_id × pizza_id line-item grain and will double-count/over-count orders that contain multiple pizzas. | Do not use when you need customer-level aggregates (e.g., total pizzas per customer) without first aggregating — using it directly will miscount because multiple rows can share the same customer_id. | Do not use as an events stream that includes runner/delivery info — it is LEFT JOINed only to pizza_names; runner/delivery fields live in pizza_runner_events_clean or pizza_order_runner_join, so relying on this view would miss or omit those cohorts. | Do not use when you need exploded/normalized exclusions or extras as separate rows — this view keeps exclusions and extras as whatever representation is in pizza_orders_base (likely delimited or nested) and will produce silently-wrong results if code expects one-row-per-exclusion or one-row-per-extra. | Do not use when you expect only matched pizza_name rows — the LEFT JOIN means pizza_name can be NULL for unmatched pizza_id; aggregations or filters that assume non-null names may silently drop or misattribute rows if NULLs are not handled.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need the raw order-level line items without the extra nullable pizza_name column — pizza_orders_base has the same order_id × pizza_id grain but avoids NULLs introduced by the LEFT JOIN. | use pizza_order_runner_join instead when you need delivery/runner context for each order line — pizza_orders_with_names lacks runner/delivery fields and will miss that cohort information. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded when you need one row per extra item — pizza_orders_with_names keeps extras as a single field, whereas pizza_get_extras_expanded reshapes extras into separate rows. | use pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you need one row per exclusion — pizza_orders_with_names preserves exclusions as-is and will cause mis-counts when code assumes exploded exclusions. | use pizza_topping_reference or pizza_recipes_base when you need canonical recipe/topping mappings rather than the user-visible pizza_name — pizza_orders_with_names only attaches pizza_name from pizza_names and does not provide recipe or topping-level detail.

views.description: Denormalized order rows joined to pizza_names to expose pizza_name for each order. Use when reporting orders by pizza type or when grouping by pizza_name. Preserves one row per order_id. | Use for: top pizzas by order count; orders per pizza_name over time; customer preferences by pizza_name

views.name: pizza_runner_events_clean
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id AS order_id,
  runner_id AS runner_id,
  pickup_time AS pickup_time,
  distance AS distance,
  duration AS duration,
  cancellation AS cancellation
FROM pizza_clean_runner_orders

params.when_to_use: When you need runner-level facts for a specific pizza order: e.g., compute metrics about a runner on an order such as that runner's pickup_time, distance, duration, or whether that runner cancelled for that order (one row per order_id × runner_id). | When joining order × runner as the atomic grain for downstream calculations (no aggregation required): e.g., listing all runners who handled each order with their associated timings and cancellation flag. | When computing aggregates that explicitly group by order_id and runner_id (for example: average duration per (order, runner) or count of runner-attempts per (order, runner)).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need order-level aggregates (one row per order): this view is at the order_id × runner_id grain and will over-count if you aggregate without removing the runner dimension (e.g., SUM(distance) or COUNT(*) per order will count each runner separately). | Do not use when you need runner-level history independent of order context (one row per runner): this view ties metrics to a particular order and cannot be used as a pure runner-timeseries without aggregating across orders. | Do not use when you need columns not present here (e.g., customer info, order totals, toppings, or recipe details): those fields are not selected from pizza_clean_runner_orders and will be missing, producing NULLs or join failures if assumed present. | Do not use when you need pre-joined human-readable names or enriched order metadata: sibling view pizza_orders_with_names provides name fields and enrichments; this view only exposes IDs and timing/distance/cancellation fields. | Do not use when you expect a deduplicated canonical order row (order-level dedupe): if pizza_clean_runner_orders contains multiple runner rows per order, this view preserves them, so using it as canonical order table will silently multiply rows.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you want canonical order-level attributes (one row per order) — pizza_orders_base has the order-level grain while pizza_runner_events_clean is at order_id × runner_id and will produce multiple rows per order. | use pizza_orders_with_names instead when you need human-readable customer or runner names and enriched order metadata — pizza_runner_events_clean exposes only IDs and timing/distance/cancellation fields. | use pizza_order_runner_join instead when you need a joined relationship between orders and runners combined with other runner or order dimension fields — pizza_runner_events_clean selects directly from pizza_clean_runner_orders and provides only the six columns shown. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded or pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you need item-level reshaped extras/exclusions for orders — those are item/ingredient-level reshapes, whereas pizza_runner_events_clean is runner-event level and contains no item/ingredient data. | use pizza_order_rank_by_time when you need ranking or analytic ordering of orders/runners by time — pizza_runner_events_clean contains raw pickup_time/duration but no precomputed rank.

views.description: Canonical runner pickup events using the cleaned runner orders table (numeric distance and duration). Exposes distance and duration as numeric measures for aggregation and includes cancellation flag. Use for runner performance and delivery time analyses. | Use for: average delivery duration/distance per runner; join runner events to orders to compute end-to-end times; cancellation rates by runner or time window

views.name: pizza_order_runner_join
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id AS order_id,
  o.customer_id AS customer_id,
  o.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  o.exclusions AS exclusions,
  o.extras AS extras,
  o.order_time AS order_time,
  r.runner_id AS runner_id,
  r.pickup_time AS pickup_time,
  r.distance AS distance,
  r.duration AS duration,
  r.cancellation AS cancellation
FROM pizza_orders_base o
LEFT JOIN pizza_runner_events_clean r ON r.order_id = o.order_id

params.when_to_use: Analyze metrics or attributes at the order × runner level — e.g., “for each order and runner pairing, show order_time, runner pickup_time, distance, duration, and whether the run was cancelled.” | Join order-level details (customer_id, pizza_id, exclusions, extras) to the runner event that attempted/handled that order (runner_id plus event timestamps and travel metrics). | Compute per-(order,runner) travel metrics or time deltas (e.g., pickup_time − order_time) when you expect at most one runner event per order or you intentionally want a LEFT JOIN that preserves orders with no runner event.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need true order-level aggregates (one row per order) — this view has grain order_id × runner_id and will duplicate order-level attributes if multiple runner events exist for the same order, producing inflated counts and wrong aggregations. | When you need runner-event-only analysis (one row per runner event) without bringing order attributes — using this view preserves order columns but may hide runner-event deduplication rules present in pizza_runner_events_clean. | When you need to restrict to successful deliveries vs. cancellations: this view includes cancellation flag from the runner event but applies a LEFT JOIN; rows with no matching runner event will appear with cancellation = NULL, which is not equivalent to cancellation = FALSE. | When you need expanded/exploded extras or exclusions as separate rows: this view keeps extras and exclusions as stored in pizza_orders_base (likely aggregated/array/text). Use the reshaped sibling views if you need one-row-per-extra or one-row-per-exclusion. | When you need normalized order metadata such as human-readable names — this view uses raw IDs from pizza_orders_base (customer_id, pizza_id) and does not include joined name lookups; using pizza_orders_with_names (if it exposes names) is better for presentation. | When deduplication of runner events is required: if pizza_runner_events_clean can contain multiple event rows per order (e.g., retries), aggregating or selecting a canonical event is necessary before reusing this join — otherwise time/distance aggregations will be silently wrong.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you want pure order-level data (no runner-event columns) — pizza_orders_base has the same order columns but avoids duplication introduced by joining runner events. | use pizza_runner_events_clean instead when you want pure runner-event-level data with any deduplication/cleaning semantics preserved — pizza_runner_events_clean contains runner_id, pickup_time, distance, duration, cancellation without attaching order attributes. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded when you need one row per extra item — pizza_order_runner_join keeps extras as a single field and will not produce exploded rows needed for item-level counts or joins. | use pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you need one row per exclusion — the joined view retains exclusions as an aggregate field, causing incorrect counts or item-level filters if reused for exclusion-level analysis. | use pizza_orders_with_names when you need human-readable names for customers or pizzas — pizza_order_runner_join only exposes customer_id and pizza_id, not names or denormalized labels.

views.description: Join of canonical orders to cleaned runner events. One row per (order_id, runner_id) representing an order with its runner pickup info. Useful for end-to-end order-runner analyses and to compute delivery metrics per order. | Use for: delivery time per order; orders without runner events; correlate order_time to pickup_time and duration

views.name: pizza_get_extras_expanded
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  row_id AS row_id,
  order_id AS order_id,
  extras AS extras,
  extras_count AS extras_count
FROM pizza_get_extras

params.when_to_use: List every individual extras row previously persisted in pizza_get_extras: use when you need one output row per extras record identified by row_id (detailed/row-level inspection or debugging). | Join-level enrichment keyed by row_id: use when you want to join on the exact extras row_id coming from pizza_get_extras and preserve that row-level multiplicity. | Extract extras text or the stored extras_count exactly as produced by pizza_get_extras without applying further aggregation (reporting the stored value or exporting raw rows).
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating extras per order (e.g., total number of extras per order) — this view is row-level by row_id, so summing extras_count here will double-count unless you first deduplicate or aggregate by order_id; using it directly for order-level aggregates yields wrong counts. | Filtering to get a cohort of orders (order-level filters) — the view returns multiple rows per order_id (if pizza_get_extras had multiple rows per order), so applying order-level WHERE logic without grouping can produce an incorrect cohort (duplicate orders). | Using extras as if it were normalized topping identifiers — extras is passed through exactly as stored; if you need exploded or normalized extra items (one row per individual topping) this view will be wrong because it preserves whatever representation pizza_get_extras uses. | Replacing pizza_orders_* views for order-level attributes (customer name, runner, timestamps) — this view only contains row_id, order_id, extras, extras_count and lacks order-level fields, so reusing it instead of pizza_orders_base or pizza_orders_with_names will omit required columns and lead to incorrect joins or NULLs. | Assuming extras_count is a reliable aggregation computed downstream — extras_count is a stored column from pizza_get_extras and may reflect the original extraction logic; do not treat it as a computed canonical aggregate without verifying how pizza_get_extras derived it.
params.comparison: use pizza_get_exclusions_expanded instead when you need the analogous reshape of exclusions rather than extras — it has the same RESHAPE pattern and row-level grain but contains exclusion-specific values rather than extras. | use pizza_orders_base when you need order-level attributes or a single row per order — pizza_orders_base is normalized to the order grain and contains many order columns that this extras view lacks. | use pizza_orders_with_names when you need order-level joins that include customer/runner names — it performs JOINs to add human-readable fields that pizza_get_extras does not provide. | use pizza_order_runner_join when you need runner-event linkage at the order grain — that view focuses on runner/event relationships and order-level joins rather than per-extras rows. | use pizza_topping_reference when you need canonical topping metadata (ids, names, categories) — pizza_get_extras stores extras text and counts but does not provide reference metadata or normalization.

views.description: Bridge table exposing extras per order in normalized form (one row per extras occurrence). Use to aggregate extras usage or join to pizza_toppings after casting extras to topping_id if needed. Preserves extras_count measure. | Use for: count extras per topping; orders with most extras; join extras to toppings dimension

views.name: pizza_get_exclusions_expanded
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  row_id AS row_id,
  order_id AS order_id,
  exclusions AS exclusions,
  total_exclusions AS total_exclusions
FROM pizza_get_exclusions

params.when_to_use: Retrieve per-row exclusion details for each row_id (one row per row_id) when you need the raw exclusions payload and the precomputed count total_exclusions exactly as stored in pizza_get_exclusions. | Join exclusions onto other tables at the same row-level grain using row_id as the join key (e.g., enrich a dataset that already has pizza_get_exclusions.row_id values). | Export or reshape exclusion rows where you do not need to recompute counts or change aggregation levels — when consumers expect the stored exclusions and the stored total_exclusions value.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to answer questions aggregated by order_id (e.g., number of exclusions per order) unless you explicitly aggregate: the view is at grain = row_id, so aggregating by order_id without re-counting may double count or undercount rows because multiple row_id values can share an order_id. | Avoid using it to define cohorts or filters by order-level attributes (for example: 'orders placed in June'); filtering/joining at order_id should be done against an order-level view (pizza_orders_base or joins) to avoid accidental row-multiplication because this view is row_id-grained. | Do not reuse this view as a source of canonical exclusion counts for different aggregation boundaries (e.g., counts per customer, per day, per runner) because total_exclusions is the value stored per row_id and may not represent the correct aggregated total for other grains. | Do not treat the exclusions column as a normalized/exploded list of one exclusion per row: the view preserves the exclusions column from pizza_get_exclusions as-is (RESHAPE label indicates transformation elsewhere), so if you need one row per single exclusion item you must reshape/explode it yourself or use a different view. | Avoid using this view to answer time-series or ranking questions — it has no time or ordering columns; using it in those contexts risks producing silently wrong results because necessary temporal grain is missing.
params.comparison: use pizza_get_extras_expanded instead when you need the equivalent reshape for extras rather than exclusions — it has the same reshaped pattern (RESHAPE) but provides extras data rather than exclusions. | use pizza_orders_base instead when you need order-level attributes or to filter by order cohorts — pizza_orders_base is NORM at the order_id grain, so joining/aggregating from there avoids row-multiplication that occurs when starting from a row_id-grained view. | use pizza_orders_with_names when you need order-level data plus customer/participant names — it is a JOIN on order-level entities (order_id grain) and prevents mistaken per-row duplication from row_id-grained sources. | use pizza_order_runner_join when you need runner-related joins at the order level — it provides JOINed relationships at a coarser grain suitable for runner/order analysis compared with this row_id-grained view.

views.description: Bridge table exposing exclusions per order in normalized form (one row per exclusion occurrence). Use to analyze common exclusions or to join to pizza_toppings when exclusions encode topping ids. | Use for: most commonly excluded toppings; orders with many exclusions; join exclusions to toppings dimension

views.name: pizza_topping_reference
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  topping_id AS topping_id,
  topping_name AS topping_name
FROM pizza_toppings

params.when_to_use: Look up the canonical metadata for a single topping by its topping_id (e.g., 'What is the name of topping_id = 42?'). | Join-on reference dimension to enrich other tables at the topping_id grain without changing row counts (e.g., LEFT JOIN to translate topping_id to topping_name). | Populate dropdowns, labels, or user interfaces that need the list of toppings and their stable identifiers.
params.when_not_to_use: Answer questions about toppings per order or per pizza — this view is at the topping_id dictionary grain, not an order- or pizza-level grain. Reusing it to count toppings per order would produce incorrect row multiplicity (it will return one row per topping, not per order). | Filter-intended cohort selection that depends on order or event attributes (for example 'toppings used in orders in June') — this view has no order/event columns and cannot restrict to a cohort; doing so would silently return the full topping set or drop intended filters. | Aggregate metrics over toppings usage (e.g., 'how many times was each topping used') — this view contains only identifiers and names, not usage counts; aggregating it will count distinct toppings rather than usage events, producing wrong totals. | Assume any temporal or runner/order context (time, order_id, runner_id) — it contains none of those dimensions, so time-based or runner-based analyses will be silently wrong if this view is reused for them. | Expect expanded or reshaped outputs (extras, exclusions, recipes) — this view does not explode or normalize multi-valued fields; using it where a reshaped set is required will miss rows and relationships.
params.comparison: use pizza_toppings (base table) instead when you need the authoritative source including any additional topping attributes not surfaced by this view — pizza_topping_reference only exposes topping_id and topping_name. | use pizza_orders_base when your analysis is at the order grain (per-order metrics, counts, or filters) — pizza_topping_reference is purely a reference dimension and will not reflect order-level multiplicity. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded or pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you need toppings as expanded per-order/per-pizza extras or exclusions — those reshaped views expose the relationship between orders/pizzas and toppings, whereas pizza_topping_reference does not. | use pizza_orders_with_names when you need order-level data with human-readable names already joined — that view joins names into orders, avoiding a separate join to the reference dimension. | use pizza_recipes_base when you need recipe-to-topping relationships or recipe-level compositions — pizza_topping_reference only provides topping metadata and not recipe membership.

views.description: Simple pass-through of topping dimension. Use to provide topping_name when joining to recipe/extras/exclusions after parsing or casting those ids. | Use for: map topping ids to names; human-readable extras/exclusions reports

views.name: pizza_recipes_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  toppings AS toppings
FROM pizza_recipes

params.when_to_use: Get attributes of a pizza recipe at the recipe (pizza) level — e.g., “what are the toppings for pizza_id = X?” | Joined as a recipe dimension when you need a 1:1 relation keyed by pizza_id (lookups, label display, enrichment of orders with recipe toppings) | Export or seed data where each row should represent exactly one recipe (one pizza_id per row) without any aggregation or duplication
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use for questions that need order- or event-level counts (e.g., number of orders containing a topping) — the view is at recipe grain, so joining it to orders without deduplicating recipe_ids can double-count orders or inflate counts. | Do not use when you need expanded rows per topping (e.g., one row per topping choice) — toppings is returned as a single field; it is not exploded/normalized, so queries expecting separate topping rows will be wrong or require additional parsing/reshape. | Do not use for cohort or temporal analyses by order or runner events — it has no order_id, customer_id, timestamp, or runner fields, so it cannot define cohorts or filter by time; using it in place of an orders/events view will produce empty or misleading cohorts. | Do not use when you need authoritative topping metadata (e.g., topping names, ids, attributes) — this view only surfaces the toppings column as stored on pizza_recipes; use the topping reference if you need normalized topping details. | Do not use when you expect aggregated summaries (counts, sums, averages) — this view contains raw recipe rows and will not provide pre-aggregated metrics; aggregations must be performed explicitly and carefully to avoid incorrect cardinality.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need order-level rows (pizza_orders_base has order_id, timestamps and order context) — pizza_recipes_base is recipe-level only and lacks order/event fields | use pizza_get_extras_expanded or pizza_get_exclusions_expanded instead when you need exploded/normalized rows for extras or exclusions — those RESHAPE views expand multi-value fields into one-row-per-item, whereas pizza_recipes_base returns toppings as a single field | use pizza_topping_reference when you need canonical topping metadata (ids, display names, attributes) — topping_reference is a NORM source of topping details; pizza_recipes_base only includes the toppings column as stored per recipe | use pizza_orders_with_names or pizza_order_runner_join when you need enriched order joins (customer/runner names or runner join context) — those JOIN views combine order and identity information which pizza_recipes_base does not contain

views.description: Canonical pizza recipes table exposing the denormalized toppings list for each pizza_id. Use as the starting point when exploding recipes into one-row-per-(pizza_id,topping) downstream (parsing required). | Use for: what toppings are on each pizza; explode recipes to count topping frequency across pizzas

views.name: trees_by_zipcode
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode AS zipcode,
  boroname AS boroname,
  COUNT(*) AS tree_count,
  AVG(tree_dbh) AS avg_tree_dbh
FROM trees
WHERE status IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY zipcode, boroname

params.when_to_use: Count and average statistics of trees broken down by zipcode and borough (boroname) for records that have a non-NULL status. Example: “How many tree records are there in each zipcode and borough, and what is the average tree_dbh for those records?” | Reporting or charting at the zipcode × borough grain where NULL status records should be excluded (status IS NOT NULL). | Generating aggregates for mapping or summary tables where each row should represent the zipcode + boroname combination and the counts/avg are computed across all matching rows in the trees table.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need counts of unique trees by an identifier (de-duplicated): this view uses COUNT(*) which counts rows, not distinct tree IDs, so it will overcount if the source has duplicate rows or multiple records per tree. | When you need aggregates across a different grain (for example: borough-only, city-wide, or individual tree level): the view groups by zipcode and boroname, so reusing it and further grouping or aggregating can produce silently wrong averages or counts unless you re-aggregate correctly (weighted averages, sum of counts, etc.). | When you need to include rows with NULL status: the view filters out status IS NOT NULL, so it will omit those trees and produce biased counts/averages if NULL-status rows should be part of the cohort. | When you need other tree attributes in the aggregation (e.g., median tree_dbh, percentiles, or distributions): this view only provides COUNT(*) and AVG(tree_dbh); those other metrics are not available and cannot be reconstructed exactly from these two numbers. | When you need zipcode or boroname resolved differently (e.g., normalized postal code formats or borough IDs): this view returns the raw zipcode and boroname columns as present in trees and may not match alternate normalized representations used elsewhere. | When combining with views at a different aggregation level (e.g., joining to per-order or per-company sibling views): directly joining aggregates at different grains can create many-to-many expansions and double counting unless you join on the exact zipcode+boroname grain and respect the filter on status.
params.comparison: use income_by_zipcode instead when you need socioeconomic metrics keyed by zipcode — it is normalized (NORM) and likely has income-specific fields; trees_by_zipcode is an aggregate (AGG) of tree counts and average DBH, not income. | use companies_funding_summary instead when you need company-level or funding aggregates — although both are AGG, companies_funding_summary aggregates over companies and financial metrics, not geographic tree counts; they differ in grain and domain. | use pizza_orders_base or other NORM sibling views when you need row-level detail (e.g., individual tree records analogous to order lines) instead of pre-aggregated counts/averages — those normalized views preserve per-record attributes and do not filter out rows by status. | use a sibling NORM view of trees (not listed here) or create a new base-level query when you need to change the filter (include NULL status) or compute distinct counts/other aggregations — trees_by_zipcode encodes a fixed WHERE and GROUP BY that cannot be changed without re-querying the raw table.

views.description: Aggregated tree counts and average diameter (tree_dbh) by zipcode and boroname. Useful for relating tree inventory to neighborhood-level statistics or income tables. | Use for: trees per zipcode; compare tree density with income or health metrics

views.name: income_by_zipcode
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode AS zipcode,
  Estimate_Total AS Estimate_Total,
  Margin_of_Error_Total AS Margin_of_Error_Total,
  Estimate_Median_income AS Estimate_Median_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Median_income AS Margin_of_Error_Median_income,
  Estimate_Mean_income AS Estimate_Mean_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Mean_income AS Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
FROM income_trees

params.when_to_use: When you need zipcode-level income estimates (total population, median, and mean) exactly as provided by the source table income_trees — i.e., to display or join a zipcode's Estimate_Total, Estimate_Median_income, and Estimate_Mean_income without further aggregation or filtering. | When you need to join zipcode-level income statistics onto another table at the zipcode grain (one row per zipcode) and you will not aggregate or re-weight those estimates across multiple zipcodes. | When you need both point estimates and their corresponding margins of error for total, median, and mean income at the zipcode level for error propagation or display alongside the estimate.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse this view when you need any aggregation across zipcodes (for example, city-, county-, or state-level averages or totals). Reason: the view is already at zipcode grain and contains point estimates per zipcode; summing or averaging those columns naively will produce silently wrong results because Estimate_* fields are precomputed estimates (and margins of error are not additive) rather than raw counts or microdata. | Do not reuse this view when you need to restrict to a different cohort than the full population represented by income_trees (for example, only households, only adults, or a demographic subgroup). Reason: the view does not include any cohort-defining columns or filters — it simply projects columns from income_trees and will not exclude or indicate subgroup membership. | Do not reuse this view when you require row-level denominators or counts used to compute the estimates (for example, to recompute margins of error, perform custom weighting, or calculate rates). Reason: the view does not expose sample sizes, weights, or the raw numerator/denominator used to derive Estimate_* and Margin_of_Error_*. | Do not reuse this view when you need a different aggregation level within the same zipcode (for example, block-group or tract within a zipcode). Reason: grain is zipcode; there is no lower-level geography available, so you cannot disaggregate without access to the source microdata. | Do not reuse this view for time-series comparisons unless income_trees and this view are known to be time-specific and include a time column. Reason: the view has no date/time column — it is static per zipcode and will lead to wrong conclusions if treated as time-indexed.
params.comparison: use trees_by_zipcode instead when you need zipcode-level aggregates computed from raw rows (for example, to recompute estimates or to get denominators) — it is an AGG sibling that may contain aggregation logic or counts missing from this NORM projection. | use companies_by_industry when your join target is company-level or industry-level rather than zipcode-level — companies_by_industry is a JOIN sibling tailored to company/industry grain, whereas income_by_zipcode is strictly zipcode grain. | use statistics_by_state_date when you need state-level or time-series statistics — statistics_by_state_date is a NORM view that includes state and date dimensions that income_by_zipcode lacks. | use a base source (income_trees) directly when you need additional fields or to apply filters not exposed here — income_by_zipcode is a column projection of income_trees and will not provide columns beyond those listed.

views.description: Household income estimates per zipcode from the income_trees table. Keeps median and mean estimates along with margin of error fields for downstream joins to trees or demographic analyses. | Use for: join income to trees by zipcode; analyze median income vs tree density

views.name: companies_funding_summary
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id AS company_id,
  valuation AS valuation,
  funding AS funding,
  select_investors AS select_investors
FROM companies_funding

params.when_to_use: When you need company-level (one row per company_id) summary fields: the company's reported valuation, the company's reported total funding, and the company's select_investors as stored in companies_funding. | When you want the raw stored values from the companies_funding table without any additional joins, filters, or recalculation. | When building a report or downstream join where company_id is the primary key and you expect exactly one row per company from this view.
params.when_not_to_use: When you need a different grain (for example, funding rounds, investor-level rows, or time-series per company) — this view is at company_id grain and will silently hide multiple rounds or per-round details. | When you need computed aggregations across companies (e.g., total funding by industry or by state) — aggregations across this view assume each company contributes one valuation/funding row; if companies_funding actually contains multiple rows per company, sums or averages will be wrong unless de-duplicated upstream. | When you need the canonical company attributes from companies_dates_base or companies_by_industry — this view only exposes columns present in companies_funding (valuation, funding, select_investors) and may omit authoritative name, founded date, industry, or other identifiers. | When you need normalized investor rows (each investor per company) or want to filter by individual investor attributes — select_investors appears to be a stored field (likely a list or preselected string); reusing it as if it were normalized investor rows will lead to incorrect joins or counts. | When you need a cleaned/validated cohort (e.g., only active companies, or companies within a date range) — this view applies no cohort filtering and will include whatever rows are present in companies_funding.
params.comparison: use companies_dates_base instead when you need authoritative company attributes (dates, canonical keys) — companies_dates_base is a base table with normalized company attributes; companies_funding contains funding-specific columns only. | use companies_by_industry instead when you need industry joins or to group/aggregate by industry — companies_by_industry provides industry context via joins, while companies_funding only provides funding-related fields. | do not substitute trees_by_zipcode or income_by_zipcode — those sibling AGG views are for geographic aggregations (different domain and grain); they are not relevant substitutes but indicate other AGG-level usage patterns in the DB.

views.description: Summary metrics per company: exposure of funding and valuation along with select_investors text. Useful as a company-level fact for joining to dates/industries or for ranking companies by funding/valuation. | Use for: rank companies by funding or valuation; join funding to company founding dates or industries

views.name: companies_dates_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id AS company_id,
  date_joined AS date_joined,
  year_founded AS year_founded
FROM companies_dates

params.when_to_use: Get one row per company with its stored join date and founding year — e.g. “For each company_id, what is date_joined and year_founded?” | Lookups or joins where you need canonical company-level attributes (company_id → date_joined, year_founded) without changing row-count or aggregating | Filtering companies by their join date or founding year when downstream logic expects one row per company
params.when_not_to_use: As a pre-aggregated source for counts or rates (e.g. “how many companies joined per year”) — WHY: this view returns one row per company, not an aggregated count per year; using it directly for aggregation risks double-counting if companies appear multiple times in source (though current schema shows one row per company, the view does no GROUP BY) | As a cohort/temporal event stream (e.g. “all company events by date”) — WHY: the view exposes only a single date_joined value per company, not multiple events or time-series rows | As a substitute for views that include joins to other entities (e.g. companies_by_industry) — WHY: this view contains only company_id, date_joined, year_founded and lacks industry or other attributes; substituting it will produce missing columns or NULLs | When you need normalized/expanded relations (e.g. exploded multi-valued fields) or derived fields (e.g. age of company computed consistently) — WHY: the view returns raw columns and performs no reshaping, derivation, or validation | When you need guaranteed uniqueness or deduplication logic beyond the source table — WHY: this view simply SELECTs from companies_dates and does not enforce uniqueness, so duplicate company_id rows in the base table would propagate and can silently change aggregates or joins
params.comparison: use companies_by_industry instead when you need company-level attributes plus industry information — it includes industry JOINs whereas companies_dates_base does not | use companies_funding_summary instead when you need aggregated funding metrics per company — it provides AGG results (funding totals) while companies_dates_base provides only raw date and year fields | use statistics_by_state_date when you need aggregated statistics by date and geography — it is an NORM view designed for time/geography aggregation, while companies_dates_base is a company-grain lookup | do not replace pizza_orders_base or other order/event-level views with this view — those sibling views have different grains (orders, events) and contain many columns needed for order/event analyses; companies_dates_base has company-level attributes only

views.description: Company date and founding-year information. Use to join with funding/industries for age-based analyses or cohorting by year_founded. | Use for: company age cohorts; join to funding to compute funding by age

views.name: companies_by_industry
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id AS company_id,
  industry AS industry
FROM companies_industries

params.when_to_use: List all company → industry pairs (one row per company_id and industry) as recorded in companies_industries. | Find the industry label(s) for a given company_id (lookup/cohort membership by company). | Join to other tables at the company_id + industry grain when you need the exact industry value that companies_industries holds.
params.when_not_to_use: If you need one row per company only (company-level deduped industry) — this view can contain multiple rows per company if a company has multiple industries; using it as if it were one-row-per-company will double-count or produce multiple matches. | If you need industry aggregates (counts, sums, or other rollups) — this view is a raw mapping and does not perform aggregation; aggregating without deduplicating can mis-count (e.g., counting rows will count company–industry pairs, not distinct companies). | If you need a canonical or current industry when companies_industries can contain historical or multiple records — this view exposes all rows from companies_industries and does not apply filters for 'current' or primary industry, so it may return outdated or secondary industries. | If you need to filter or join on companies that satisfy other cohorts (for example only funded companies or companies with dates) — this view has no filters and will include all rows from companies_industries, so using it as a pre-filtered cohort is unsafe. | If you expect normalized/enriched company attributes (names, funding summary, dates) — this view only surfaces company_id and industry and does not join to company metadata, so it cannot answer questions requiring those attributes.
params.comparison: use companies_dates_base instead when you need company-level temporal filters (e.g., 'companies active in 2020') — companies_dates_base has company date attributes and is one-row-per-company context, whereas companies_by_industry is a raw company↔industry mapping. | use companies_funding_summary instead when you need aggregated funding metrics per company or to restrict to funded companies — companies_funding_summary provides aggregated funding info and a company-level grain, whereas companies_by_industry is unaggregated and may have multiple rows per company. | use statistics_by_state_date or trees_by_zipcode when you need pre-aggregated geographic summaries — those sibling views are aggregations (AGG) at their respective grains; companies_by_industry is not aggregated and only contains company↔industry pairs.

views.description: One row per company-industry association. Use to group or filter companies by industry or to join industry labels to funding/dates. | Use for: funding by industry; count companies per industry

views.name: statistics_by_state_date
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  date AS date,
  state AS state,
  total_cases AS total_cases,
  total_deaths AS total_deaths
FROM statistics

params.when_to_use: When you need raw per-day, per-state cumulative totals already present in the underlying table (e.g., 'What were the reported total_cases and total_deaths for each state on each date?'). | When you want a 1:1 projection of the statistics table filtered or joined later by downstream logic (this view does no aggregation or filtering itself). | When you need columns named date, state, total_cases, total_deaths exactly for downstream convenience or to standardize column names across queries.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need a different aggregation level (for example national totals by date or weekly sums). This view is at the grain ['date','state'] and performs no aggregation — aggregating it without care can double‑count or undercount if there are multiple rows per (date,state) in the base table. | Do not use this view to compute rates, deltas, or per-capita metrics (for example new_cases per day, case growth, or cases per 100k) because the view exposes only the raw total_cases and total_deaths; it does not contain prior-day values or population denominators required to compute those metrics. | Do not reuse this view as a pre-filtered cohort (for example 'only confirmed cases' or 'only states in region X'). The view applies no filters — using it as if it were already filtered will silently include all rows from statistics. | Do not assume uniqueness of rows per (date, state). If the underlying statistics table can contain multiple rows for the same date and state (different sources, versions, or splits), aggregating this view without deduplication may produce incorrect sums. | Do not use this view when you need enriched reference data (for example state names, region codes, or population). This view only projects columns present in the statistics table and does not join to any reference tables.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need a similarly raw, base-level projection of another domain — it is also NORM and exposes base table columns without joins or aggregation; statistics_by_state_date differs because it contains epidemiological totals (date/state/total_cases/total_deaths) rather than order data. | use pizza_orders_with_names or pizza_order_runner_join when you require joined/enriched data (they are JOIN views). Those sibling views already incorporate related tables; statistics_by_state_date is a simple projection and does not perform joins, so prefer a JOIN sibling when you need enrichment such as region metadata or population. | use trees_by_zipcode or companies_funding_summary when you intend to work with pre-aggregated data (AGG siblings). Those views perform aggregation at their declared grain; statistics_by_state_date is not aggregated beyond projecting existing columns, so for ready-made aggregated insights prefer the AGG siblings.

views.description: Pass-through of state-level statistics by date. Exposes total_cases and total_deaths per date and state for trend analyses. | Use for: trend of cases/deaths by state over time; compute growth rates between dates

views.name: pizza_order_rank_by_time
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id AS order_id,
  customer_id AS customer_id,
  pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  order_time AS order_time,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_time) AS order_rank
FROM pizza_orders_base

params.when_to_use: Find the per-customer ordinal position of each order when ordering that customer's orders by order_time (e.g., "what number order is this for the customer?"). | Return one row per order_id enriched with the rank of that order within the same customer ordered by order_time (useful for churn/retention analyses that need the sequence position). | Filter or join by order_rank to select first/second/... orders per customer (after applying the same order_time criteria used in this view).
params.when_not_to_use: When you need a different grain than order_id (e.g., one row per customer, per pizza_id, or per order_time bucket): this view is strictly order-level and will produce duplicate/irrelevant rows or require additional aggregation. | When you need a dense integer sequence without gaps (DENSE_RANK): this view uses RANK(), which can produce ties and skip numbers; using it when you expect contiguous sequence numbers will silently produce gaps. | When you need ranking across a different partition/cohort (e.g., ranking across all customers, by pizza_id, by delivery zone): this view always partitions by customer_id, so cross-customer or alternate-cohort ranks will be wrong. | When you need deterministic tie-breaking beyond order_time (e.g., stable ordering for equal order_time values): ties in order_time will produce equal ranks; if you need a unique order per rank you must include additional ORDER BY expressions before applying ranking. | When you need enriched customer or pizza attributes (names, recipe details, toppings, runner events): this view only surfaces IDs and order_time; reusing it expecting names or JOINed attributes will force extra joins or lead to semantic mistakes if joins change the ranking. | When you need the original unsuffixed aggregates (counts, sums) or expanded reshape outputs from related reshape/aggregation views: this view does not aggregate or reshape extras/exclusions and will not substitute for those summaries.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need the raw order rows without any ranking — pizza_orders_base is the source used to compute ranks and preserves original columns without windowing. | use pizza_orders_with_names instead when you need human-readable customer or pizza names alongside ranking — pizza_orders_with_names already joins name fields, avoiding extra joins that could alter filtering/order semantics. | use pizza_get_extras_expanded or pizza_get_exclusions_expanded when you need per-order expanded extras/exclusions — those reshape views provide the exploded attributes that this rank view does not contain. | use a view/window with DENSE_RANK() (not provided in siblings) or construct a custom window over pizza_orders_base when you require contiguous rank numbers without gaps — pizza_order_rank_by_time uses RANK() which allows gaps on ties. | use pizza_order_runner_join or pizza_runner_events_clean when your ranking or sequence logic must consider runner/delivery events or tie-breakers based on runner timestamps — they contain runner event data not present in this view.

views.description: Rank orders per customer by order_time (1 = earliest). Useful to compute first/most recent orders per customer or to filter to first/last events downstream by applying WHERE order_rank = 1 or <= K. | Use for: first order per customer; most recent or nth order per customer (apply WHERE order_rank <= K or = N)
